question: A 40-year-old is found unconscious after an alleged assault. CT scan shows a biconvex (lenticular) hyperdense collection between the skull and dura. The most likely diagnosis and the vessel most commonly responsible are:

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Subdural haematomas appear as crescent-shaped collections following the brain contour and are caused by torn bridging veins. A biconvex collection is the hallmark shape of an extradural, not subdural, haematoma.

Correct. An extradural haematoma is classically biconvex (lens-shaped) because the dura is stripped from the inner table of the skull by an arterial bleed. The middle meningeal artery, running in the pterion region, is the vessel most commonly torn — typically by a temporal bone fracture. The classic lucid interval precedes rapid deterioration.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage appears as diffuse hyperdensity in the subarachnoid spaces (basal cisterns, sulci) on CT, not a focal biconvex collection. It is more commonly due to ruptured berry aneurysm in spontaneous cases.

Intracerebral haematoma appears as an intraparenchymal hyperdense lesion within the brain substance, not a biconvex extra-axial collection. Lenticulostriate artery involvement is typical in hypertensive bleeds.

overallFeedback.feedback: The shape of the collection is the diagnostic key: biconvex = extradural (arterial, middle meningeal); crescent = subdural (venous, bridging veins). These distinctions carry medicolegal weight regarding mechanism and survivability.

Excellent analysis. The biconvex shape is the key morphological feature of extradural haematoma — the rigid dura limits spread to create the lens shape. Always correlate with temporal bone fracture and ask about the lucid interval in history.
